original_text: To make the simulation computationally feasible, we will use an "extended atom" model, where hydrogen atoms are implicitly combined with the heavy atoms to which they are bonded. This simplification reduces the number of interactions and eliminates high-frequency vibrations, permitting larger time steps in the integration of the equations of motion.
modified_text: To focus on the functionally relevant slow dynamics, we will use an "extended atom" model, where hydrogen atoms are implicitly combined with the heavy atoms to which they are bonded. This simplification correctly filters out the high-frequency, non-diffusional vibrations of hydrogen atoms, permitting a clearer analysis of the underlying fluid-like motions.
explanation: The mechanism of this error is a flawed theoretical assumption embedded in the simulation model. The modified text reframes a computational shortcut as a physically justified "filter." While the "extended atom" model is a standard approximation, it is not a perfect physical filter. By removing explicit hydrogen atoms and their associated hydrogen bonds, the model can significantly alter the potential energy surface, making it more rugged and artificially restricting the very motions it is meant to study. This can inhibit the subtle rearrangements necessary for fluid-like, diffusional behavior. The flaw lies in the unsubstantiated claim that this simplification "correctly filters" the dynamics, when in fact it may be introducing an artifact that pre-determines a non-diffusional, solid-like result, thereby invalidating any conclusion about the hypothesis.
reasoning: The error relies on a contested term ("correctly filters") where its operationalization (removing explicit hydrogens) diverges from its intended meaning (physically justified filtering of high-frequency noise without altering underlying dynamics).
